overview:
Ancala Gaccha (often spelled Anchal Gaccha or Achal Gaccha; Hindi: अंचलगच्छ / अचलगच्छ) is a monastic lineage within the Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka tradition of Jainism. In classical and modern sources it is also called Vidhipakṣa Gaccha, a name that emphasizes its self-understanding as a community of monks committed to strict adherence to the canonical prescriptions (vidhi) and monastic discipline. As one of the historically important gacchas (orders) among the Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka, it participates fully in image-venerating temple worship while simultaneously stressing rigorous observance of ascetic rules.

Historically, Ancala Gaccha traces its origin to the reform movement led by Ācārya Aryarakṣitasūri (Aryarakshitsuri) in the late 11th and early 12th centuries CE, in the wider context of medieval Jainism in Gujarat and Rajasthan under the Caulukya (Solanki) rulers. According to traditional narratives and later historical reconstructions, Aryarakṣitasūri was initially an ācārya in an older lineage (often connected to the Vada Gaccha or Bṛhadgaccha). Disturbed by what he perceived as laxity and compromise in monastic practice—especially regarding rules on water usage and other ascetic disciplines—he relinquished his earlier leadership title and undertook a program of reform. The group of monks who accepted his stricter code of conduct came to be known as Vidhipakṣa Gaccha, and over time the order acquired the names Achal/Anchal Gaccha through both legendary and epigraphically attested usage.

Traditional accounts preserved in later samācārī (disciplinary) texts and historical works describe Aryarakṣitasūri as codifying a detailed set of rules and ritual prescriptions for the Vidhipakṣa Gaccha. These rules were intended to restore what he regarded as the "true path" of Jain monasticism, grounded in the Āgamas. The reform attracted a large following: some narratives report thousands of ascetics—monks and nuns—within the order, and note that several other gacchas (such as Śaṅkheśvar Gaccha, Vallabhi Gaccha, Nadol Gaccha, and others) either fully or partially adopted the Vidhipakṣa samācārī and merged into the lineage. While exact numbers and dates vary across sources, the broad picture is of a reformist movement that consolidated multiple strands of Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka monasticism under a stricter disciplinary regime.

The names "Achal" and "Anchal" are explained through different narrative traditions. One widely circulated legend connects "Achal" (meaning "firm, unwavering") to an episode involving King Jayasiṃha Siddharāja of Gujarat. During a royal sacrifice (putrakāmeṣṭi yajña), a cow is said to have died from a snakebite within the ritual enclosure, threatening the success of the rite. Aryarakṣitasūri, using the esoteric practice of parakāya-praveśinī (entering another body), is said to have revived the cow, thereby fulfilling his promise and earning the epithet "Achal" for his steadfastness. Another tradition, often considered closer to epigraphic evidence, links the name "Anchal Gaccha" to a courtly episode under King Kumārapāla, where a lay devotee purified the ground by touching it with the end (añcala) of his upper garment before bowing to Aryarakṣitasūri; impressed by this ritual gesture and its scriptural sanction (as confirmed by the scholar Hemacandra), the king is said to have associated the order with the term "añcala". In inscriptions and historical records, "Anchal Gaccha" appears as a common designation, suggesting that this second explanation aligns more closely with documentary evidence, while the first functions primarily as hagiographic narrative.

Within the broader Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka framework, Ancala Gaccha shares the doctrinal foundations of Jainism: belief in the eternal jīva (soul), the reality of karma, the path of right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct, and the ultimate goal of liberation (mokṣa). Its distinctive emphasis lies in monastic discipline and ritual correctness. Sources describing the Vidhipakṣa samācārī highlight strict rules on water (boiling and filtration), careful observance of vows related to non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possession, and detailed regulations for daily conduct, alms rounds, and temple-related activities. These rules are presented as a return to the prescriptions of the canonical texts, rather than as innovations, and thus the order positions itself as conservative and reformist at the same time—conservative in its appeal to scripture, reformist in its critique of contemporary laxity.

Over the centuries, Ancala Gaccha produced and transmitted a body of literature in Prakrit, Sanskrit, and later vernacular languages, including samācārī texts, question-and-answer manuals, ritual guides, and historical narratives. Works such as the "Praśnottara-paddhati" (Śatpadikā) attributed to Dharmaghoṣasūri, and later compilations of Vidhipakṣa samācārī, systematize the disciplinary code and provide practical guidance for monks and nuns. Modern scholarly studies and community histories—such as "Achalgaccha kā Itihās" and reviews of Vidhipakṣa samācārī texts—draw on manuscripts, inscriptions, and oral traditions to reconstruct the lineage’s development, its mergers with other gacchas, and its regional spread in Gujarat, Rajasthan, and Maharashtra.

In the contemporary period, Ancala Gaccha remains a numerically modest but active lineage within the Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka community. Leadership titles such as gacchādhipati (head of the order) continue to be used, and recent acharyas have worked to maintain the Vidhipakṣa emphasis on strict discipline while engaging with modern educational institutions and lay communities. The order’s monks and nuns participate in temple worship, scriptural teaching, and community guidance, but any formal religious rulings or life-changing decisions (such as dīkṣā, prolonged fasting, or medical choices) are understood, within Jain tradition, to require consultation with qualified living teachers and appropriate professional experts. From a historical and academic perspective, Ancala Gaccha offers a case study in how Jain monastic lineages negotiate continuity and reform, scriptural authority and lived practice, and hagiographic memory and documentary evidence.

Because many of the narratives about Ancala Gaccha—especially miracle stories and precise numerical claims—derive from later hagiographies and community histories, scholars distinguish between primary textual evidence (such as inscriptions and early samācārī manuals) and later legendary elaboration. Where inscriptions and dated manuscripts confirm names, titles, and basic chronological frameworks, they provide stronger historical grounding. Where only oral tradition or late compilations exist, historians treat the material as reflecting community self-understanding rather than verifiable fact. A careful study of Ancala Gaccha therefore involves reading primary texts, traditional commentaries, and modern scholarship together, noting points of agreement, areas of uncertainty, and the ways in which the lineage’s identity has been shaped over time.

primary_sources.title: Daśavaikālika-sūtra (as cited in Aryarakṣitasūri’s reform narratives)
primary_sources.author: Canonical Śvetāmbara Jain scripture; specific reform interpretation attributed to Aryarakṣitasūri
primary_sources.original_text: जले न स्पृशेत् न पिबेत् अचुल्लं (paraphrased canonical idea: a monk should not touch or drink unboiled water; exact canonical wording varies by edition and is not reproduced here verbatim).
primary_sources.transliteration: jale na spṛśet na pibet acullaṃ (paraphrastic rendering, not a critical edition line).
primary_sources.translation: “A monk should neither touch nor drink water that has not been properly treated (boiled/filtered).” (Interpretive translation summarizing the rule that inspired Aryarakṣitasūri’s concern about lax practice.)
primary_sources.notes: This entry represents the canonical rule on water usage that, according to later narratives, Aryarakṣitasūri encountered while revising the Daśavaikālika-sūtra. In the story, he questions why monks are using unboiled water despite the scriptural prohibition. The precise Sanskrit/Prakrit wording differs across critical editions, so the line given here is a paraphrase rather than a verbatim quotation. The narrative context is preserved in later biographies and histories of Aryarakṣitasūri (corpus tier B–D), which interpret the canonical rule as the catalyst for the Vidhipakṣa reform movement.

primary_sources.title: Praśnottara-paddhati (Śatpadikā) of Dharmaghoṣasūri
primary_sources.author: Dharmaghoṣasūri (Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka monk of the Vidhipakṣa/Ancala Gaccha)
primary_sources.original_text: ṇaṃ bhikkhūṇaṃ samācāriyaṃ evaṃ bhavadi (Prakrit-style formulation summarizing monastic conduct; exact manuscript readings vary and are not standardized here).
primary_sources.translation: “Thus, the proper conduct (samācārī) of monks is as follows.”
primary_sources.notes: The Praśnottara-paddhati, also known as Śatpadikā, is a question-and-answer manual attributed to Dharmaghoṣasūri, an early successor in the Vidhipakṣa/Ancala Gaccha lineage. It systematizes monastic discipline in a concise format, reflecting the order’s emphasis on strict adherence to rules. The line given here is a representative, paraphrastic opening formula indicating that the text sets out the samācārī of monks. Critical editions and manuscript studies (corpus tier A–C) provide more precise readings; the present entry highlights the genre and function of the text rather than reproducing it in full.

primary_sources.title: Inscriptions and historical records referring to “Anchal Gaccha”
primary_sources.author: Various royal and community scribes; preserved in stone and metal inscriptions
primary_sources.original_text: … अंचलगच्छस्य आचार्य आर्यरक्षितसूरिणः … (formulaic Sanskrit/Prakrit inscriptional reference; exact wording varies by inscription).
primary_sources.translation: “… of Ācārya Aryarakṣitasūri of the Anchal Gaccha …”
primary_sources.notes: Epigraphic records from medieval Gujarat and Rajasthan include references to Ācārya Aryarakṣitasūri and the Anchal (Ancala) Gaccha, often in the context of temple donations, image installations, or royal grants. These inscriptions provide primary evidence for the use of the name “Anchal Gaccha” and for the historical presence of the lineage in specific regions and periods. The formula cited here is a composite representation of typical inscriptional language; individual inscriptions differ in detail. Scholars use these records (corpus tier A–C) to corroborate or correct later narrative accounts about the origin and naming of the gaccha.

primary_sources.title: Achalgaccha kā Itihās (History of the Achalgaccha)
primary_sources.author: Dr. Shivprasad
primary_sources.original_text: अचलगच्छ (विद्हिपक्ष) श्वेताम्बर मूर्तिपूजक समाज का एक महत्त्वपूर्ण गच्छ है, जिसकी स्थापना आचार्य आर्यरक्षितसूरि द्वारा विधिमार्ग के प्रवर्तन से हुई।
primary_sources.transliteration: achalagaccha (vidhipakṣa) śvetāmbara mūrtipūjaka samāja kā ek mahatvapūrṇa gaccha hai, jisakī sthāpanā ācārya āryarakṣitasūri dvārā vidhimārga ke pravartana se huī.
primary_sources.translation: “Achalgaccha (Vidhipakṣa) is an important gaccha of the Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka community, whose establishment took place through the promulgation of the path of prescribed conduct (vidhimārga) by Ācārya Aryarakṣitasūri.”
primary_sources.notes: This modern Hindi scholarly work (corpus tier C–D) synthesizes manuscript evidence, inscriptions, and traditional narratives to present a historical account of the Achal/Ancala Gaccha. The quoted sentence illustrates how the author frames the lineage as both significant within the Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka community and defined by its emphasis on vidhimārga. While not a primary canonical text, the book is an important secondary source for understanding the order’s self-presentation, the chronology of its development, and the historiographical debates about its naming and mergers with other gacchas.

primary_sources.title: Vidhipakṣagacchna Samācārī Grantho ane Vidhiras: Ek Samīkṣā
primary_sources.author: Muni Kalāprabhasāgar (Kalaprabhsagarji)
primary_sources.original_text: विद्हिपक्ष (अंचल) गच्छ के समाचारी ग्रन्थों और विधिरस का यह समालोचनात्मक अध्ययन उनके इतिहास, विकास और साहित्यिक योगदानों पर प्रकाश डालता है।
primary_sources.transliteration: vidhipakṣ (añcal) gaccha ke samācārī granthoṃ aur vidhiras kā yah samālocanātmaka adhyayan unke itihās, vikās aur sāhityik yogadānoṃ par prakāś ḍāltā hai.
primary_sources.translation: “This critical study of the samācārī texts and the Vidhiras of the Vidhipakṣa (Anchal) Gaccha sheds light on their history, development, and literary contributions.”
primary_sources.notes: This modern review (corpus tier C–D) examines the disciplinary texts (samācārī granthas) and ritual manuals (Vidhiras) of the Vidhipakṣa/Ancala Gaccha. It provides an overview of the lineage’s internal literature, its codification of rules, and its historical evolution. The quoted sentence is a representative summary of the work’s purpose. While not itself a primary canonical source, it is valuable for mapping the relationship between early samācārī texts, later commentaries, and contemporary practice within the gaccha.

misconceptions.myth: Ancala Gaccha is a completely separate sect of Jainism, unrelated to the main Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka tradition.
misconceptions.reality: Ancala Gaccha is a monastic lineage within the Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka tradition, sharing its core doctrines, temple-based image worship, and canonical foundations. Its distinctiveness lies in its emphasis on strict monastic discipline and adherence to scriptural prescriptions (vidhimārga), not in a separate doctrinal system or independent sectarian identity.

misconceptions.myth: The miracle stories about Aryarakṣitasūri—such as reviving a cow through parakāya-praveśinī—are established historical facts that define the origin of the name “Achal Gaccha.”
misconceptions.reality: Miracle narratives about Aryarakṣitasūri belong to the hagiographic layer of the tradition. While they are important for understanding how the community remembers and honors its founder, they are not independently verifiable historical events. Epigraphic and manuscript evidence more reliably attests to the use of the name “Anchal Gaccha” and to the existence of the lineage, whereas the specific miracle stories function as devotional and didactic tales rather than critical historical data.

misconceptions.myth: Because Ancala Gaccha stresses strict discipline, it rejects or minimizes temple worship and image veneration.
misconceptions.reality: Ancala Gaccha is part of the Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka community, which is characterized precisely by image-venerating temple worship. The gaccha’s emphasis on discipline concerns how monks and nuns conduct themselves—rules about water, vows, daily routines, and ritual correctness—rather than a rejection of mūrti-pūjā. Its monastics participate in temple rituals in accordance with the lineage’s samācārī and the broader Mūrtipūjaka framework.

misconceptions.myth: All numerical claims about the number of monks and nuns in Ancala Gaccha at its peak (for example, thousands of ascetics) are precise and unquestionable historical statistics.
misconceptions.reality: Traditional accounts often present large numbers of monks and nuns to emphasize the success and influence of the Vidhipakṣa reform. These figures, however, come from later narrative sources and may be idealized or symbolic. Historians treat them cautiously, cross-checking them against inscriptions, dated colophons, and other documentary evidence. The general picture of a substantial following is plausible, but exact numbers should be regarded as approximate rather than strictly verified.

misconceptions.myth: Modern lay Jains can safely adopt any ascetic practice mentioned in Ancala Gaccha narratives (such as prolonged fasting or extreme austerities) without further guidance, because the lineage is known for strict discipline.
misconceptions.reality: Jain tradition, including Ancala Gaccha, distinguishes clearly between monastic and lay obligations. Extreme austerities, prolonged or waterless fasting, and practices approaching sallekhana require careful discernment, health considerations, and guidance from qualified living teachers, as well as appropriate medical and professional advice. Historical and hagiographic descriptions of ascetic practices are not direct prescriptions for contemporary lay life. Responsible application of Jain ethics always involves attention to bodily health, family responsibilities, and professional counsel.
